name: Turbo-Base64
workload: Single-threaded base64 encode/decode with error checking, buffer sizes from 4 bytes to 1 MB and 30 MB binaries, across x86 SSE/AVX/AVX2/AVX512VBMI, ARM Neon, and PowerPC Altivec
claimed_speedup: On i7-9700k (gcc 11.2), AVX2 tb64v256 hits 29086/29748 MB/s encode/decode on 1MB buffers vs aklomp b64avx2's 26153/22515 MB/s and lemire fastbase64 fb64avx2's 23686/21231 MB/s; on 4-16B short strings tb64v256 AVX2 hits 2330/2161 MB/s vs aklomp's 891/734 MB/s (~2.6-2.9x); on AMD Ryzen 9 7950X (gcc-12.2) AVX512VBMI hits 77619/76716 MB/s encode/decode on 1MB buffers, beating memcpy's 37047/31694 MB/s
compiler_and_flags: gcc 11.2 (i7-9700k table), gcc-12.2 (AMD Ryzen 9 7950X table), clang 12.0 (Apple M1 table), clang 6.0 (ARMv8 A73 table)
hardware: Intel i7-9700k 3.6GHz; AMD Ryzen 9 7950X @4.5GHz DDR5-6000 CL30; Apple M1 3.5GHz; ARMv8 A73 ODROID-N2 1.8GHz
tradeoffs: GPLv3 (separate commercial license available); runtime CPU dispatch picks scalar/SSE/AVX/AVX2/AVX512 path; RISC-V currently falls back to the generic scalar core with no dedicated RVV backend
caveats: Benchmark table is the project author's own README, not an independent third party, but hardware and compiler are stated per row so it meets tier A

name: base64-turbo (hacer-bark)
baseline: base64 (RFC 4648), measured directly against Turbo-Base64 (C), the prior fastest known base64 codec
workload: criterion.rs benchmark (benches/encoding_bench.rs), base64 encode/decode across input sizes 32B-10MB, pinned to one core
claimed_speedup: At 64KiB: base64-turbo 81.6/106.5 GiB/s (enc/dec) vs Turbo-Base64's 80.7/107.8 GiB/s on AWS c8a.large (AMD EPYC 9R45); 25.7/36.9 GiB/s vs Turbo-Base64's 18.2/38.5 GiB/s on c7i.large (Intel Xeon Platinum 8488C); full sweep peaks at 123.0 GiB/s encode and 118.1 GiB/s decode at 4KiB on c8a.large
compiler_and_flags: rustc via `cargo bench` (release/opt-level 3, criterion.rs, 5s warmup/15s measurement); MSRV 1.93.0; Turbo-Base64 built from its own upstream C source with its official build
hardware: AWS c8a.large (AMD EPYC 9R45, Zen5) and c7i.large (Intel Xeon Platinum 8488C, Sapphire Rapids), pinned to one core
tradeoffs: Pure Rust; SIMD kernels use `unsafe` verified with Kani/MIRI/MSan/fuzzing, scalar fallback is `#![forbid(unsafe_code)]`; no published C API/bindings, so a C++ caller would need to write its own FFI shim; custom (non-RFC4648) alphabets lose AVX2/NEON acceleration
caveats: 0BSD carries no explicit patent grant; results vs Turbo-Base64 are mixed (decode is slightly slower on both tested machines, encode is faster); extremely new and low-visibility (2 stars, first commit ~2026-01), not yet independently reproduced, and the benchmark was run and published by the same author who wrote the crate
found_via: GitHub: gh api graphql search query "turbo base64"

name: base64simd (WojciechMula)
workload: SIMD (SSE/AVX2/AVX512F/AVX512BW/AVX512VBMI/BMI2/ARM Neon) base64 encode/decode vs scalar baseline; per-machine numbers live in the repo's results/ subdirectories
claimed_speedup: Vectorized encoding 2-4x faster than scalar; decoding 2-2.7x faster than scalar, depending on CPU architecture
stars_or_usage: 172 stars; algorithms adopted by aklomp/base64 and Turbo-Base64
tradeoffs: Research/reference code (verify/check/speed/benchmark programs per ISA), not a packaged library API; AVX512 variants need Intel SDE to test without native hardware
caveats: This is the reference implementation behind the peer-reviewed paper 'Faster Base64 Encoding and Decoding Using AVX2 Instructions' (Muła & Lemire, ACM Transactions on the Web, arXiv:1704.00605), which is why it is tier B; the top-level README states only a speedup range, not a specific CPU/compiler — exact per-machine numbers are in results/ files that were not individually opened this session
found_via: GitHub: gh api repos/WojciechMula/base64simd (surfaced via aklomp/base64 and Turbo-Base64 acknowledgements)

name: fastbase64 (lemire)
baseline: base64 (glibc/Linux base64 utility and Google Chrome's base64 implementation)
workload: 1MB and 50,000-byte buffer base64 encode/decode, benchmarked third-party inside powturbo/Turbo-Base64's benchmark suite
claimed_speedup: fb64avx2 (AVX2) hits 23686/21231 MB/s enc/dec on 1MB buffers vs 'linux' base64's 1754/219 MB/s (~13x/97x) and Chrome's base64 2541/4289 MB/s (~9x/5x) on Intel i7-9700k gcc 11.2; on ARMv8 A73 fb64neon reaches 512/782 MB/s vs Linux's 314/91 MB/s
tradeoffs: No declared license (NOASSERTION) — can be studied/reimplemented but not copied; project archived, no further maintenance
caveats: Evidence comes from a third party's (Turbo-Base64) benchmark harness rather than fastbase64's own repo, but that harness states compiler and CPU, meeting tier A; fastbase64 itself loses to both Turbo-Base64 and aklomp/base64 in that same table, so it is still much faster than plain/Linux/Chrome but not the fastest option found
found_via: GitHub: gh api repos/lemire/fastbase64 (referenced in Turbo-Base64 README 'References')

name: base64 (aklomp)
baseline: base64 (plain/bytewise scalar encode-decode, the 'Plain' column in its own benchmark table)
workload: 10MB buffer base64 encode/decode across community-submitted machines (x86/ARM/PowerPC), plus a buffer-size sweep on an i7-4770
claimed_speedup: On i5-4590S @3.0GHz: AVX2 enc/dec 4160/6344 MB/s vs Plain 3356/3197 MB/s (~1.2x/2x); SSSE3 4363/6104 MB/s vs Plain (~1.3x/1.9x). On i7-4770 @3.4GHz with buffer size tuned to the 100KB-1MB cache window, AVX is 12x faster than Plain, reaching 24/27 GB/s (derived from page data)
hardware: i5-4590S @3.0GHz; i7-4770 @3.4GHz DDR1600 (buffer-size sweep); various community-submitted CPUs in the table
stars_or_usage: 1022 stars; used as the comparison baseline by Turbo-Base64 and cited across the base64-SIMD ecosystem
tradeoffs: Optional OpenMP path adds parallel speedup but adds a dependency; many rows in its own table are flagged '*: Update needed' by maintainers; ARM NEON support is a compile-time toggle, not runtime detection
caveats: No compiler version stated in the benchmark table, and several rows are explicitly marked stale by the maintainers, so capped at tier C per the unstated-flags rule
found_via: GitHub: gh api repos/aklomp/base64 (surfaced via Turbo-Base64 references)

name: simdutf
baseline: base64 (WHATWG forgiving-base64 / RFC 4648; the repo's own benchmark harness links libbase64 (aklomp), OpenSSL 3, and Node.js's base64 as named competitors)
workload: binary-to-base64 and base64-to-binary conversion; repo ships benchmarks/base64/benchmark_base64.cpp which builds against libbase64_spaces.h (aklomp), openssl3_base64.h, and node_base64.h as competitors
claimed_speedup: README states the library 'transcodes a billion characters per second or more' and is '3 to 10 times faster than ICU' (20x on easy/ASCII strings) — that headline figure is for general Unicode transcoding vs ICU, not base64-specific; the dedicated base64 benchmark tool exists and links the named base64 competitors, but no head-to-head base64 throughput table is published in the README itself
compiler_and_flags: requires a recent C++ compiler and CMake with -D SIMDUTF_BENCHMARKS=ON, built in release mode per repo instructions; no specific compiler/version pinned in README
stars_or_usage: 1979 stars; base64/UTF routines shipped in Node.js, WebKit/Safari, Chromium, Bun, Ladybird, Cloudflare Workers
tradeoffs: Large, actively used multi-purpose codec (UTF-8/16/32 + Latin1 + Base64 + encoding detection); adopting it for base64 alone pulls in a bigger surface than a single-purpose codec
caveats: Confirmed the benchmark harness directly compiles against aklomp/base64, OpenSSL3 and Node's base64 as named competitors, but did not find a published results table with exact base64 throughput numbers in the README opened this session — numbers must be reproduced locally with `benchmark_base64`. Do not conflate the ICU-comparison figures (UTF-8/16/32) with base64 performance
found_via: GitHub: gh api graphql search query "simdutf"

name: fast-hex (zbjornson)
workload: Encoding/decoding byte buffers to/from hex strings using AVX2, standalone C++ module and Node.js binding, benchmarked against a scalar loop
claimed_speedup: C++: decoding ~12.5x over scalar, encoding ~11.5x over scalar. Node.js binding: ~2.12x faster decode for short inputs (<1,031,913 chars), ~12x faster decode for some long strings/Buffers/TypedArrays, ~5.5x faster encode
compiler_and_flags: Requires AVX2 (-march=haswell on GCC/Clang/ICC, /arch:AVX2 or EnableAdvancedInstructionSet on MSVC); exact compiler version not stated
tradeoffs: Does not validate input by design (documented limitation, PR welcome to add it); requires AVX2 (Haswell or later), no documented fallback path for older CPUs
caveats: Numbers are the author's own claim in the README; no CPU model, compiler version, or raw MB/s figures given, only ratios, so capped at tier C
found_via: GitHub: gh api graphql search query "hex encoding simd fast"

name: crc-fast (awesomized/crc-fast-rust)
baseline: CRC32 (specifically CRC-32/ISCSI aka crc32c, and CRC-32/ISO-HDLC aka crc32; README's own numeric comparison is against the Rust `crc` crate's ~0.5 GiB/s default)
workload: 1KiB and 1MiB buffer CRC calculation (CRC-32/ISCSI, CRC-32/ISO-HDLC, CRC-64/NVME, CRC-32/BZIP2, CRC-64/ECMA-182) via SIMD (AVX-512 VPCLMULQDQ/PCLMULQDQ on x86_64, NEON+PMULL(+SHA3) on aarch64)
claimed_speedup: Up to >220x faster than the default Rust `crc` crate (~0.5 GiB/s); CRC-32/ISCSI reaches ~111 GiB/s (1MiB) on Intel Sapphire Rapids (avx512-vpclmulqdq) and ~99 GiB/s on Apple M3 Ultra (neon-pmull-sha3); CRC-32/ISO-HDLC reaches ~88 GiB/s on Sapphire Rapids and ~98 GiB/s on M3 Ultra
compiler_and_flags: cargo build --release (rustc, stable-2 MSRV policy); exact rustc version/flags used for the perf table not stated
hardware: AWS EC2 c7i.metal-24xl (Intel Sapphire Rapids), c7a.metal-48xl (AMD Genoa), c8g.metal-48xl (AWS Graviton4), c6g.metal (Graviton2), Apple M3 Ultra (Mac Studio 32-core), Apple M4 Max (MacBook Pro 16" 16-core)
stars_or_usage: 94 stars; used by aws-smithy-checksums (AWS SDK for Rust) and a PHP extension
tradeoffs: Core implementation is Rust, but it ships a C/C++-compatible dynamic and static library plus an auto-generated header via its `ffi` feature, so C++ callers get a real linkable ABI rather than just source
caveats: The >220x figure is against a Rust crate, not a C library like zlib/glibc — no direct zlib comparison was found in the README; the detailed GiB/s table only shows this library's own numbers per platform (no baseline column), so the ratio can't be independently re-derived from that table alone
found_via: GitHub: gh api graphql search query "crc32 simd"

name: crc32c (htot)
baseline: CRC32 (CRC-32C/Castagnoli; SlicingBy8 software baseline is representative of the algorithm used by most CRC32 library implementations)
workload: 4096-byte buffer CRC32C benchmark comparing Sarwate, SlicingBy4, SlicingBy8, Adler, Hardware32, Hardware64 (SSE4.2 crc32 instruction) and IntelC (crc32 + pclmulqdq) implementations on i7 and Intel Edison
claimed_speedup: On 64-bit i7: SlicingBy8 is 5.1x faster than Sarwate; Hardware64 is 4.2x faster than SlicingBy8; IntelC is 2.7x faster than Hardware64 (derived from page data: roughly ~58x faster than the Sarwate byte-at-a-time baseline). On 32-bit Intel Edison, IntelC is 8.8x faster than SlicingBy8
compiler_and_flags: make all (optimizations on by default per README; exact compiler/version not stated); DEBUG=TRUE builds an unoptimized debug variant
hardware: generic "i7" (exact model not stated); Intel Edison @ ~500MHz (32-bit and 64-bit); NUC E3815
license: BSD-2-Clause (stated in README; not machine-detected by GitHub's license API)
tradeoffs: IntelC path is only efficient above 216-byte buffers due to pclmulqdq combine overhead; 32-bit portability path needs inline assembly; unmaintained since 2017
caveats: CPU model for the main comparison is only given as generic 'i7' with no frequency or compiler version; the compared implementations (Sarwate/SlicingBy8/Hardware/IntelC) are all bundled in this same repo rather than an external library like zlib, so the 'CRC32 baseline' here is this project's own software CRC32 variants, not a third-party incumbent
found_via: GitHub: gh api graphql search query "crc32c"
